title: Waves
lead: A wave is a disturbance that moves away from the place where it was created, and the water wave is the easiest one to picture. This section defines the wave velocity and the wavelength, shows that the wave travels one wavelength in the time of one period, so that its speed is the wavelength divided by the period and also the frequency times the wavelength, and separates the two kinds of wave: the transverse wave, whose disturbance is across the direction of travel, and the longitudinal wave, whose disturbance is along it.
objectives: State the characteristics of a wave.
Calculate the velocity of wave propagation.
summary_html:
• A wave is a disturbance that moves from the point of creation with a wave velocity $\kvw$.
  • A wave has a wavelength $\klam$, which is the distance between adjacent identical parts of the wave.
  • Wave velocity and wavelength are related to the wave’s frequency and period by $\kvw = \frac{\klam}{\kT}$ or $\kvw = \kf\klam.$
  • A transverse wave has a disturbance perpendicular to its direction of propagation, whereas a longitudinal wave has a disturbance parallel to its direction of propagation.

(Figure 16.29) In this example of a transverse wave, the wave propagates horizontally, and the disturbance in the cord is in the vertical direction. (Figure 16.30) In this example of a longitudinal wave, the wave propagates horizontally, and the disturbance in the cord is also in the horizontal direction.

exercises.prompt: Why is it important to differentiate between longitudinal and transverse waves?

answer.solution: In the different types of waves, energy can propagate in a different direction relative to the motion of the wave. This is important to understand how different types of waves affect the materials around them.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between the waves coming from a tuning fork and electromagnetic waves?

answer.solution: The waves coming from a tuning fork are mechanical waves that are longitudinal in nature, whereas electromagnetic waves are transverse in nature.

exercises.prompt: Represent longitudinal and transverse waves in a graphical form.

answer.solution: Draw the direction of propagation first, as an arrow pointing to the right, and then draw the disturbance against it. For the transverse wave, draw a cord along that direction and displace it up and down, so that the shape is a sine curve of wavelength $\klam$ whose crests and troughs lie a distance $\kX$ above and below the undisturbed line; the disturbance is perpendicular to the arrow. For the longitudinal wave, draw a row of evenly spaced coils along the same direction and move each one back and forth along the line, so that the coils bunch together at the compressions and spread apart between them; the disturbance is parallel to the arrow, and the wavelength is the distance from one compression to the next. In both drawings the amplitude $\kX$ is the greatest distance a piece of the medium is moved from its undisturbed place.

exercises.prompt: Why is the sound produced by a tambourine different from that produced by drums?

answer.solution: The sound energy coming out of an instrument depends on its size. The sound waves produced are relative to the size of the musical instrument. A smaller instrument such as a tambourine will produce a high-pitched sound (higher frequency, shorter wavelength), whereas a larger instrument such as a drum will produce a deeper sound (lower frequency, longer wavelength).

exercises.prompt:
A transverse wave is traveling left to right. Which of the following is correct about the motion of particles in the wave?
(a) The particles move up and down when the wave travels in a vacuum.
(b) The particles move left and right when the wave travels in a medium.
(c) The particles move up and down when the wave travels in a medium.
(d) The particles move right and left when the wave travels in a vacuum.

answer.solution: Choice (c). In a transverse wave the disturbance is perpendicular to the direction of propagation, so a wave travelling left to right moves the particles up and down, which rules out (b) and (d). The particles are pieces of a medium, and a mechanical wave such as this one needs a medium to travel through, so (a), which puts the particles in a vacuum, describes nothing that could carry the wave.

exercises.prompt: The graph shows propagation of a mechanical wave. What is the wavelength of this wave?

answer.hint: Read off the distance from one crest to the next.

exercises.prompt: Give one example of a transverse wave and another of a longitudinal wave, being careful to note the relative directions of the disturbance and wave propagation in each.

answer.solution: A wave on a guitar string is transverse: the wave runs along the string, while the string itself moves across that direction, perpendicular to the way the wave travels. A sound wave in air is longitudinal: the wave travels away from the speaker, and the air is pushed back and forth along that same line, so that the disturbance is parallel to the direction of propagation.

exercises.prompt: What is the difference between propagation speed and the frequency of a wave? Does one or both affect wavelength? If so, how?

answer.solution: The propagation speed $\kvw$ is how fast the disturbance itself moves through the medium, and it is set by the medium. The frequency $\kf$ is how many times a second a piece of the medium goes through a complete cycle, and it is set by whatever makes the wave. Both affect the wavelength, because $\kvw = \kf\klam$, so $\klam = \kvw/\kf$. For a given medium, shaking faster gives a shorter wavelength; for a given frequency, a medium that carries the wave faster gives a longer one.

exercises.prompt: Storms in the South Pacific can create waves that travel all the way to the California coast, which are 12,000 km away. How long does it take them if they travel at 15.0 m/s?

answer.hint: The distance divided by the speed gives the time in seconds; turn that into days.

exercises.prompt: Wind gusts create ripples on the ocean that have a wavelength of 5.00 cm and propagate at 2.00 m/s. What is their frequency?

answer.hint: Rearrange $\kvw = \kf\klam$ for the frequency, with the wavelength in meters.

exercises.prompt: Scouts at a camp shake the rope bridge they have just crossed and observe the wave crests to be 8.00 m apart. If they shake the bridge twice per second, what is the propagation speed of the waves?

answer.hint: The crests are a wavelength apart and the shaking rate is the frequency, so use $\kvw = \kf\klam$.

exercises.prompt: What is the wavelength of an earthquake that shakes you with a frequency of 10.0 Hz and gets to another city 84.0 km away in 12.0 s?

answer.hint: Find the propagation speed from the distance and the time first, then use $\klam = \kvw/\kf$.

exercises.prompt: Your ear is capable of differentiating sounds that arrive at the ear just 1.00 ms apart. What is the minimum distance between two speakers that produce sounds that arrive at noticeably different times on a day when the speed of sound is 340 m/s?

answer.hint: The extra distance the second sound covers is the speed of sound multiplied by the smallest time difference the ear can tell apart.
